Founded in the early 20th century as a mining outpost, it grew rapidly after the discovery of vast copper deposits that made the region one of the world’s major mineral producers. Today the city blends colonial-era architecture with bustling markets, lively cafés and a growing arts scene; visitors can stroll along its tree-lined avenues, sample hearty Congolese cuisine, and feel the vibrant energy of a place that is both a commercial hub and a gateway to the country’s mineral heartland.

lbv.name: Libreville
lbv.text: Libreville, the capital of Gabon, sits on the Atlantic coast at the mouth of the Komo River in central West Africa. It began in 1849 as a settlement for freed slaves returning from Brazil, giving the town its name – “free city” – and grew into the country’s main port. Today the city blends modern high-rise offices with colourful markets where vendors sell fresh fish, tropical fruit and woven crafts. The waterfront promenade offers views of palm-lined beaches and the occasional sailboat, while cafés serve Congolese-style coffee and the nightlife buzzes around the lively neighbourhoods of the former French quarter.

lda.name: Luanda
lda.text: Luanda, the bustling capital of Angola, sits on a sweeping bay of the Atlantic Ocean at the mouth of the Cuanza River. Founded by the Portuguese in 1575, the city grew around a fortified harbour that later became a key point in the trans-Atlantic slave trade before evolving into a modern oil-driven economy. Today visitors find a lively mix of sleek skyscrapers and colourful colonial architecture, lively fish markets where the day's catch is grilled on the spot, and a vibrant nightlife along the waterfront promenade, all set against warm, tropical breezes.

lhw.name: Lanzhou
lhw.text: Lanzhou, the capital of Gansu Province in north-western China, sits on the banks of the mighty Yellow River where the Loess Plateau meets the desert fringe. Founded over two thousand years ago, it became a key hub on the ancient Silk Road, linking Chinese heartlands with Central Asia. Today the city blends modern high-rise towers with bustling night markets; you can sip freshly-made Lanzhou beef noodle soup beside the river promenade, explore the colourful Zhongshan Bridge, or take a short bus ride to the striking Bingling Grottoes perched on the cliffs of the nearby Liujiaxia Reservoir. The mix of history, culture and striking scenery makes a visit both lively and memorable.

lil.name: Lille
lil.text: Lille sits in the far north of France, just a short train ride from the Belgian border and a stone’s throw from the coast of the North Sea. Founded as a Roman settlement, it later became the capital of French Flanders and was a key stronghold during the Wars of Religion, when the city’s famous citadel was constructed by Vauban in the 17th century. Today Lille buzzes with a lively mix of historic cobbled streets, sleek modern boutiques and bustling markets; its cafés spill onto the Grand Place, and the vibrant cultural scene – from museums to street art – makes wandering its neighbourhoods a delight for any traveller.

liv.name: Liverpool
liv.text: Liverpool sits on the western edge of the Mersey Estuary in north-west England, its waterfront stretching along the River Mersey. Historically it grew into a major global port in the 18th and 19th centuries, famously serving as the gateway for many emigrants to the New World and for the trans-Atlantic trade that shaped the city’s wealth. Today the city buzzes with music, sport and culture: you can wander the historic Albert Dock, admire the impressive waterfront UNESCO World Heritage sites, enjoy lively pubs and cafés, and catch the vibrant street art and festivals that give Liverpool its warm, welcoming character.

lko.name: Lucknow
lko.text: Lucknow, the capital city of Uttar Pra Pradesh in northern India, rests on the banks of the gently flowing Gomti River and lies about 500 kilometres east of New Delhi. Historically it was the centre of the 1857 Indian Rebellion and later became renowned for its Nawabi culture, evident in the elegant architecture of the Bara Imambara and the bustling markets of Aminabad. Today, visitors find a lively mix of old and new: colonial-era streets lined with chic cafés, fragrant street-food stalls serving kebabs and biryani, and tranquil gardens where you can watch locals go about their day against a backdrop of grand monuments and modern malls.

lln.name: Lilongwe
lln.text: Lilongwe, the bustling capital of Malawi, sits in the central plateau of the country where the Lilongwe River meets the expansive, gently rolling landscape of the Central Region. Established as a colonial administrative centre in the early 1900s, it became the official capital after independence, replacing Zomba in 1975. Today the city offers a relaxed yet lively atmosphere: modern cafés line the colourful streets of the Old Town, the bustling Saturday market overflows with fresh produce and crafts, and the nearby Lilongwe Wildlife Centre provides close encounters with rescued native animals. Visitors enjoy a blend of Malawian hospitality, urban growth, and easy access to surrounding wildlife reserves.

lma.name: Lima
lma.text: Lima, the bustling capital of Peru, lies on the central western coast where the desert meets the Pacific Ocean, its skyline framed by the towering Andes to the east. Founded by Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro in 1535, the city became the centre of the Viceroyalty of Peru and retains a rich colonial heritage evident in the stone façades of its historic centre, a UNESCO World Heritage site. Today Lima teems with contrast: colourful neighbourhoods such as Barranco offer bohemian cafés and street art, while sleek skyscrapers house modern offices, and the nearby cliffs provide spectacular sunset views over the sea.

lon.name: London
lon.text: London, the capital of the United Kingdom, sits on the River Thames in southeastern England, straddling both banks of the waterway. Founded by the Romans as Londinium around AD 43, the city grew into a bustling medieval port and later the heart of the British Empire. Today, London feels like a vibrant mosaic of history and modernity: you can stand beneath the towering glass of the Shard, wander the historic cobbles of Covent Garden, and hear the chime of Big Ben while sipping a coffee in a bustling café. Museums, parks, theatres and diverse neighbourhoods make every visit feel fresh and exciting.

lpg.name: Las Palmas
lpg.text: Las Palmas, the sun‑kissed capital of Gran Canaria, sits on the island’s northeastern coast where the Atlantic meets volcanic hills and golden beaches. Founded in 1478 by Spanish conquistadors as “Real Villa de La Luz,” the city grew from a modest fishing port into a bustling entrepôt, its historic Vegueta district preserving cobblestone streets and Moorish‑influenced architecture. Today, Las Palmas is a vibrant cultural hub—home to lively markets, world‑class museums, and the famed Las Canteras promenade—while serving as a modern gateway for tourism, commerce, and renewable‑energy innovation across the Canary archipelago. Join us as we explore its timeless charm and forward‑looking spirit.

lsk.name: Lusaka
lsk.text: Lusaka, the bustling capital of Zambia, sits in the south-central part of the country on a plateau about 1,300 metres above sea level. Founded in 1905 as a modest railway depot, it became the capital of the British protectorate of Northern Rhodesia in 1911 and later of independent Zambia in 1964. Today the city blends modern skyscrapers with colourful markets, and a walk through the lively downtown reveals street food stalls, the National Museum’s exhibits on Zambian heritage, and the leafy expanse of the Lusaka National Park on the city’s edge, offering a warm, welcoming atmosphere for visitors.

lvg.name: Livingstone
lvg.text: Livingstone sits on the north-western edge of Zambia, right on the banks of the mighty Zambezi River and just a short drive from the spectacular Victoria Falls, one of the world’s largest waterfalls. The town was founded in 1905 and named after the famed explorer David Livingstone, whose grave lies a few kilometres downstream at the Old Drift. Today, Livingstone is a lively hub for tourists: the streets buzz with markets selling handmade crafts, riverside cafés offer views of the river’s mist, and a range of lodges and activity operators make it easy to experience safaris, white-water rafting and sunset cruises on the Zambezi.

lxr.name: Luxor
lxr.text: Luxor, perched on the east bank of the Nile in southern Egypt, is the modern name for the ancient city of Thebes, once the capital of the New Kingdom and home to the grand temples of Karnak and Luxor. It boasts the world-famous Valley of the Kings across the river, where pharaohs such as Tutankhamun were laid to rest. Today the town hums with a lively mix of bustling souks, rooftop cafés and river ferries, while the stone monuments glow in the desert light, offering visitors a striking blend of ancient wonder and contemporary Egyptian hospitality.

lyo.name: Lyon
lyo.text: Lyon, nestled at the confluence of the Rhône and Saône rivers in east-central France, is the country’s third-largest city and a historic crossroads of trade. Founded by the Romans as Lugdunum in 43 BC, it later became a key centre of the silk industry in the 19th century, a heritage still visible in its traboules—hidden passageways linking the old neighbourhoods. Today the city buzzes with a vibrant culinary scene, from bustling bouchons serving traditional Lyonnaise dishes to Michelin-starred restaurants, while its UNESCO-listed old town offers cobbled streets, Renaissance architecture and stunning views from the hilltop Basilica of Notre-Dam de Fourvière.

mad.name: Madrid
mad.text: Madrid, the vibrant capital of Spain, sits in the heart of the Iberian Peninsula on the Manzanares River, surrounded by the rolling Castilian plains. Founded as a modest fortress in the ninth-century, it became the royal seat when King Philip II moved his court there in 1561, establishing the city as the centre of the Spanish Empire. Today the city buzzes with a mix of historic grandeur and modern energy: you can stroll through the leafy Retiro Park, admire world-class art in the Prado, savour tapas in lively plazas, and feel the warm, cosmopolitan rhythm that makes Madrid a favourite stop for travellers.

man.name: Manchester
man.text: Manchester, nestled in the north-west of England on the River Irwell, grew from a modest medieval market town into a powerhouse of the Industrial Revolution, famously pioneering cotton spinning and railway engineering in the 19th century. Today the city buzzes with a vibrant mix of culture and sport: you can explore world-class museums such as the Science and Industry Museum, savour street food in the bustling Curry Mile, and feel the electric atmosphere of a match at the iconic Old Trafford. Its leafy canals, modern architecture and lively music scene make Manchester a friendly, energetic stop for any traveller.

mar.name: Marseille
mar.text: Marseille, perched on the southeastern coast of France where the Mediterranean meets the Rhône-Alpes region, is France’s oldest city, founded by Greek sailors from Phocaea around 600 BC. Its historic Vieux-Port still bustles with fishing boats and cafés, while the striking basilica of Notre-Dame de la Garde watches over the harbor from its hilltop perch. Today the city mixes vibrant street art, lively markets selling olives and bouillabaisse, and a lively waterfront promenade that leads to modern museums and sandy beaches. The blend of ancient stone streets, multicultural flavours and stunning sea views makes a visit feel both timeless and refreshingly contemporary.

mau.name: Maun
mau.text: Maun, situated on the banks of the Thamalakane River in north-west Botswana, is the principal gateway to the Okavango Delta and a short drive from the sprawling Makgadikgadi salt pans. The town began as a modest settlement in the early 20th century, serving as a trading post and later a colonial administrative centre before evolving into a tourism hub. Today, Maun hums with colourful market stalls, river-front cafés and a bustling airstrip that dispatches mokoro-sailing trips and game-viewing safaris into the delta’s winding waterways, offering a warm, laid-back base for adventurers.

mba.name: Mombasa
mba.text: Mombasa, Kenya’s second-largest city, sits on a low-lying peninsula jutting into the Indian Ocean on the country’s southeast coast, just a short distance north of the equator. The town grew around the historic Swahili trading settlements and was fortified by the Portuguese in 1593 when they built Fort Jesus, a UNESCO World Heritage site that still dominates the waterfront. Today visitors can wander the narrow lanes of Old Town with its Arab-influenced architecture, relax on white-sand beaches such as Diani and Nyali, enjoy fresh seafood in bustling markets, and take boat trips to the nearby marine park, where colourful coral reefs teem with life.

mbm.name: Mbuji-Mayi
mbm.text: Mbuji-Mayi, the capital of Kasai-Oriental province in the heart of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, lies on the Sankuru River about 300 km south-west of the national capital Kinshasa. Formerly called Bakwanga, the town grew rapidly after independence because it sits above one of the world’s richest diamond deposits and became the centre of the state-run Société Minière de Bakwanga. Today visitors find a city of wide avenues and colourful markets where traders sell fresh produce, fabrics and locally-cut diamonds; the pace is relaxed, the streets are lined with modest shops and cafés, and the surrounding countryside offers chances to see traditional Kasai villages and the rolling savannah beyond.

mcb.name: Maracaibo
mcb.text: Maracaibo is a bustling city in northwestern Venezuela, perched on the western shore of Lake Maracaibo and framed by the Sierra de Perijá mountains. Founded in 1529, it became an early centre of the Spanish colonial oil trade, and its historic Plaza Bolívar still bears the name of the liberator who visited the town. Today visitors find a lively mix of modern skyscrapers and colourful colonial buildings, bustling markets selling fresh fish and arepas, and the famous “Cerro de la Cruz” viewpoint that offers sweeping sunsets over the lake. The warm, humid climate and friendly locals make it a vibrant gateway to the region’s natural and cultural attractions.

mci.name: Kansas City
mci.text: Kansas City, straddling the border between Missouri and Kansas in the American Midwest, sits on the confluence of the Missouri and Kansas rivers. Founded in the early 19th century, the city grew around the historic Santa Fe Trail, which made it a key gateway for westward expansion. Today visitors enjoy a vibrant mix of jazz clubs, world-class barbecue joints and impressive art installations such as the towering “Lion” sculpture in the downtown plaza. The River Market district offers bustling farmers’ markets and historic warehouses converted into cafés, while the nearby Country Club Plaza delights shoppers with its Spanish-style architecture and lively street ambience.

mco.name: Orlando
mco.text: Orlando lies in the heart of central Florida, roughly midway between the Atlantic coast and the Gulf of Mexico and about an hour’s drive north of the bustling city of Tampa. Founded in the late 19th century, the town grew around the citrus industry and was officially incorporated in 1875; its name honours a soldier who fought in the Second Seminole War. Today the city is synonymous with world-class theme parks such as Walt Disney World and Universal Studios, but it also offers vibrant dining precincts, leafy lakeside parks and a lively arts scene, making it a colourful and welcoming destination for visitors of all ages.

mde.name: Medellin
mde.text: Medellín sits in a lush valley in the Andes of north-west Colombia, about 150 km south of the Caribbean coast and surrounded by towering mountains that give the city its nickname, the “City of Eternal Spring.” Founded in 1616, it later became the centre of a famous flower-growing region and, in the mid-20th century, was the stronghold of notorious drug cartels before undergoing a remarkable urban transformation. Today visitors find a vibrant mix of modern tramways, colourful street art, bustling markets and excellent coffee shops, all set against a backdrop of verdant hills and a pleasantly mild climate.

mem.name: Memphis
mem.text: Memphis, Tennessee, lies on the mighty Mississippi River in the southwestern corner of the state, bordering Arkansas. Founded in 1819 and named after the ancient Egyptian city, it quickly became a crucial river port and a crossroads of American culture. Today the city buzzes with the legacy of blues and rock ’n’ roll: you can stroll down historic Beale Street, visit the iconic Graceland home of Elvis Presley, and explore the National Civil Rights Museum at the former Lorraine Motel. With its lively music venues, riverfront parks and famous barbecue, Memphis feels both steeped in history and unmistakably vibrant.

mil.name: Milan
mil.text: Milan, in the north-west of Italy, sits in the fertile Po Valley between the Alps and the Adriatic Sea. First mentioned in a 6th-century Lombard document, the city became a major centre of the Renaissance, home to Leonardo da Vinci’s “The Last Supper” and the magnificent Gothic cathedral, the Duomo. Today Milan buzzes with a sleek blend of historic grandeur and modern style: you can wander its elegant arcades, sip espresso in bustling cafés, explore world-class museums, and shop the latest fashions in the vibrant Quadrilatero della Moda, all while enjoying a lively, cosmopolitan atmosphere.

mmk.name: Murmansk
mmk.text: Murmansk sits on the Kola Bay at the entrance to the Barents Sea, far above the Arctic Circle on Russia’s north-western coast. Founded in 1916 as a supply port for the war effort, it became the only ice-free harbour in the Soviet north, playing a crucial role in both World Wars and the Cold War naval fleet. Today the city greets visitors with colourful wooden houses, a bustling waterfront promenade, and the striking Alyosha monument overlooking the sea. In summer the midnight sun brightens the streets, while winter offers chances to see the Northern Lights and sample hearty Arctic cuisine in cosy cafés.

mpt.name: Maputo
mpt.text: Maputo, the vibrant capital of Mozambique, lies on the Indian Ocean coast at the southern tip of the country, where the Maputo River meets the sea. Founded as a Portuguese trading post in the 18th century, it became the colonial capital of Portuguese East Africa before independence in 1975. Today the city mixes art-deco architecture with bustling markets, palm-lined promenades and lively cafés serving piri-piri chicken and fresh seafood; a short walk takes you from the historic Praça da Independência to the colourful, fragrant streets of the Baixa district, offering a warm, relaxed atmosphere for visitors.

mqx.name: Mekelle
mqx.text: Mekelle, the capital of Ethiopia’s Tigray Region, lies on the high plateau of northern Ethiopia at about 2,500 metres above sea level, roughly 780 km north-north-east of Addis Ababa. Historically it was the seat of Emperor Yohannes IV, who ruled the country from the late 19th century until his death in 1889, and it later became an important administrative centre during the Imperial era. Today the city offers a lively market where traders display woven textiles, spices and coffee

mrk.name: Marrakesh
mrk.text: Marrakesh, set at the foothills of the Atlas Mountains in western Morocco, is a bustling gateway to the desert and a former imperial capital founded in the 11th century by the Almoravid dynasty. Its historic medina, a UNESCO World Heritage site, still winds around the famous Jemaa el-Fna square where storytellers, musicians and food stalls create an ever-changing street-performance theatre. Today the city blends traditional souks selling spices, carpets and lanterns with sleek cafés, modern hotels and vibrant art galleries, offering visitors a lively mix of old-world charm and contemporary comfort.

msp.name: Minneapolis
msp.text: Minneapolis, a vibrant city in the Upper Midwest of the United States, sits on the banks of the Mississippi River where it meets the scenic Chain of Lakes. Founded in the 1850s, it grew rapidly as a centre for flour milling, once boasting the world’s largest grain processing capacity and earning the nickname “Mill City.” Today visitors enjoy a blend of modern art, bustling food markets and extensive parkland: the Walker Art Center and its iconic Spoonbridge sculpture, the lively North Loop eateries, and miles of bike-friendly trails that wind through lush lakes and riverfront promenades, offering a fresh, lively urban experience.

msr.name: Misrata
msr.text: Misrata, a bustling coastal city on Libya’s central Mediterranean shore, sits about 150 km east of the capital Tripoli and is the country’s third-largest urban centre. Historically it was a key trading port in the Ottoman era, supplying grain and dates to ships crossing the sea. Today the city blends its lively market streets, where vendors sell fresh seafood and traditional sweets, with a modern waterfront promenade offering cafés, palm-shaded walkways and views of the sparkling harbour. Visitors can feel the hum of everyday Libyan life, explore the nearby ruins of ancient settlements and enjoy the warm, welcoming atmosphere of a city that’s both historic and forward-looking.

mta.name: Matadi
mta.text: Matadi, a bustling port town on the western edge of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, sits at the mouth of the Congo River about 150 km from Kinshasa and just a short distance from the Atlantic coast. Founded in the early 1880s as a key terminus for the railway that linked the interior to the sea, it grew into the country’s main gateway for imports and exports. Today visitors find a lively waterfront lined with colourful markets, colonial-era buildings and lively cafés, while the humid climate and constant river traffic give the town a vibrant, slightly chaotic charm that feels both historic and unmistakably modern.

muc.name: Munich
muc.text: Munich sits in the heart of Bavaria, in southern Germany, nestled between the Alpine foothills and the River Isar. First mentioned in records from the 12th century, the city grew around a Benedictine monastery and later became the seat of the Wittelsbach dukes, giving it a rich imperial heritage visible in the grandeur of the Residenz palace. Today Munich is a lively mix of tradition and modernity: you can wander the historic Marienplatz, sip a fresh lager in a bustling beer garden, explore world-class museums, and enjoy easy access to nearby mountains for a day of hiking or skiing.

nan.name: Nantes
nan.text: Nantes, situated on the banks of the Loire in western France, is a vibrant city that blends river-side charm with a rich maritime heritage. Once the historic capital of the Duchy of Brittany and a major port for Atlantic trade, its legacy is still visible in the impressive Château des Ducs de Bretagne and the preserved 18th-century shipyards of the Cité des Congrès. Today visitors can wander along the lively quays, explore the whimsical Machines of the Isle of Nantes with its giant mechanical elephant, and enjoy bustling markets, cafés and contemporary art galleries that give the city a lively, modern feel.

nap.name: Naples
nap.text: Naples, perched on the western edge of the Bay of Naples in southern Italy, is a bustling port city that has watched history unfold for over two millennia. It was a major centre of the Roman Republic and later the capital of the Kingdom of Naples, giving the region its name. Today the streets pulse with energy: you can wander past vibrant markets selling fresh mozzarella and espresso, explore the UNESCO-listed historic centre with its baroque churches and underground catacombs, and gaze across the water to the looming silhouette of Mount Vesuvius, still reminding visitors of the city’s dramatic past.

nas.name: Nassau
nas.text: Nassau, the bustling capital of the Bahamas, sits on New Providence Island just off the north-east coast of the main Bahamian archipelago, overlooking the turquoise waters of the Atlantic. Founded in the 17th century, the town became a notorious pirate haven in the early 1700s, a colourful chapter reflected in the historic Parliament Square and the famous pirate-themed museum on Bay Street. Today visitors stroll along the vibrant waterfront, browse colourful market stalls selling conch and locally-made crafts, and relax on nearby Cable Beach, while the city’s pastel colonial buildings and lively music scene give a warm, laid-back island feel.

nbo.name: Nairobi
nbo.text: Nairobi, the bustling capital of Kenya, sits in the south-central part of the country on the high-land plateau of the Great Rift Valley, at an altitude of about 1,795 metres. Founded in 1899 as a railway depot on the Uganda Railway, it quickly grew into a major administrative centre and was declared the capital of the British East Africa Protectorate in 1907. Today the city blends modern skyscrapers with lively markets, lush parks such as the Nairobi National Park where rhinos roam on the city’s edge, and a vibrant food scene that offers everything from traditional Kenyan dishes to international cuisine, making it a dynamic base for exploring East Africa.

nhv.name: Newhaven
nhv.text: Newhaven is a small coastal town in East Sussex, perched on the mouth of the River Ouse where it meets the English Channel, just a short drive east of Brighton. It grew around a medieval fishing harbour that later became an important packet-boat terminal for cross-Channel services in the 19th century, and the town’s historic harbour walls still echo that maritime past. Today visitors can stroll along the lively promenade, watch the ferries to Dieppe, enjoy fresh seafood in cosy pubs, and take in sweeping sea views from the nearby cliffs, all in a relaxed, friendly atmosphere.

nia.name: Niamey
nia.text: Niamey, the capital of Niger, sits on the banks of the winding Niger River in the country's far-southwest, close to the border with Burkina Faso. It grew from a modest French colonial outpost founded in the early 1900s and was officially made the capital of French Upper Volta in 1926, a status it retained after independence. Today the city buzzes with colourful markets where traders sell everything from woven fabrics to fresh mangoes, while the National Museum offers insight into the region’s rich cultural heritage. Strolling along the riverfront at sunset, you’ll feel the warm hospitality of a town that blends traditional life with the energy of a growing West African hub.

nic.name: Nice
nic.text: Nice, perched on the sun-kissed French Riviera between the Mediterranean Sea and the foothills of the Alps, is a vibrant coastal city in the southeast of France. It grew from a small fishing settlement into a fashionable resort after the railway arrived in 1864, attracting artists and aristocrats alike. Today the promenade along the famous Baie des Anges is lined with palm trees, cafés and the iconic pebble beach, while the narrow streets of the old town reveal colourful baroque houses, bustling markets and the scent of socca. Visitors can stroll the promenade, explore museums such as the Musée Matisse, and enjoy the blend of French and Italian influences that give Nice its distinct charm.

nkc.name: Nouakchott
nkc.text: Nouakchott, the capital of Mauritania, lies on the edge of the Atlantic Ocean in the far west of the Sahara, where the desert meets the sea. Founded in 1958 as the new administrative centre after French colonial rule, it quickly grew into the country’s main port and political hub. Today the city feels relaxed yet bustling: wide, palm-lined avenues lead to a lively fish market where fresh catches are sold, the freshly painted Museum of Black Africa showcases local heritage, and the nearby beaches offer gentle waves against a backdrop of low-rise modernist buildings and expansive dunes.

nkg.name: Nanjing
nkg.text: Nanjing, situated on the lower reaches of the Yangtze River in eastern China, was the capital of several Chinese dynasties and the seat of the early Republic of China, famously hosting the 1912 provisional government. Today the city blends its deep history with a lively modern vibe: you can wander along the historic city wall, explore the solemn Memorial Hall of the Nanjing Massacre, and then relax in bustling pedestrian streets lined with cafés, boutique shops and neon-lit skyscrapers. The surrounding Qinhuai River area offers charming lantern-lit night walks, while nearby Purple Mountain provides peaceful trails and spectacular views over the urban landscape.

nng.name: Nanning
nng.text: Nanning, the capital of Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region in southern China, sits on the banks of the Nan River a few hundred kilometres from the Vietnamese border. Historically it served as a regional administrative centre during the Tang dynasty and later became the seat of the provincial government after the establishment of the People’s Republic. Today the city is celebrated for its lush, tree-lined streets and plentiful parks, earning it the nickname “Green City”. Visitors can wander the lively Qingxiu Mountain, sample the spicy Zhuang cuisine in bustling night markets, and enjoy a relaxed blend of modern malls and traditional riverfront scenery.

nou.name: Nouadhibou
nou.text: Nouadhibou, Mauritania’s second-largest city, sits on the Atlantic coast at the western tip of the Sahara, just north of the border with Western Sahara. It began life as the French colonial settlement of Port-Étienne in the early 1900s, growing around a modest fishing harbour that later became a hub for exporting the country’s iron ore. Today the town bustles with colourful markets, bustling fish stalls and the striking “ship graveyard” where rusting hulls line the shoreline. Visitors can enjoy fresh seafood, watch lively dhow crews at work and feel the quiet expanse of the desert meeting the sea.

npr.name: Napier
npr.text: Napier, perched on the edge of Hawke Bay on New Zealand’s North Island, first grew as a modest 19th-century settlement before a devastating magnitude-7.8 earthquake in 1931 razed much of the town. The rebuilding gave it the world-renowned Art Deco façade that still lines its streets, making it a living museum of the style. Today the city buzzes with cafés, boutique shops and vibrant markets, while its sun-washed beaches and nearby vineyards draw both locals and travellers seeking fine wine, coastal walks and a taste of heritage.

nuk.name: Nukus
nuk.text: Nukus, the capital of Uzbekistan’s autonomous Republic of Karakalpakstan, lies on the banks of the Amu Darya in the far west of the country, close to the Turkmen border and the edge of the Kyzylkum desert. Founded in the late-19th century as a small settlement, it became the regional centre when the Karakalpak Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic was created in 1932. Today the town is famous for the Savitsky Museum, which houses one of the world’s largest collections of Soviet-era avant-garde art, and its wide, tree-lined streets provide a surprisingly relaxed base for exploring nearby desert landscapes and the historic fortress of Khiva.

okc.name: Oklahoma City
okc.text: Oklahoma City lies in the heart of the American Midwest, perched on the banks of the North Fork of the Canadian River in the state of Oklahoma. Founded during the Land Run of 1889, the city grew rapidly as a centre for cattle trading and later for oil production, shaping its rugged frontier character. Today it offers a lively blend of modern culture and historic charm: the vibrant Bricktown entertainment district buzzes with restaurants and river-front walks, the impressive National Cowboy & Western Heritage Museum showcases Western art, and spacious parks provide a welcoming atmosphere for visitors of all ages.

oma.name: Omaha
oma.text: Omaha, Nebraska, sits on the western bank of the Missouri River at the heart of the Midwestern United States, roughly three-hundred miles north of Kansas City. Founded in 1854 as a frontier outpost, it quickly became a key stop on the Oregon Trail and later the eastern terminus of the first transcontinental railroad, cementing its role in westward expansion. Today the city blends river-front charm with a lively cultural scene: the historic Old Market district offers cobbled streets, independent shops and cafés, while the Henry Doorly Zoo, modern museums and a bustling riverwalk give visitors a pleasant mix of nature, history and contemporary Midwestern hospitality.

osl.name: Oslo
osl.text: Oslo, Norway’s capital, sits at the head of the Oslofjord, framed by forested hills and islands that spill into the sea. First mentioned in medieval sagas, the city grew around the royal estate of Oslo founded in the 11th century and later became the seat of Norway’s government. Today it feels refreshingly compact and modern, with a lively waterfront lined with museums, cafés and sleek architecture such as the opera house’s sloping marble roof. You can stroll through Vigeland’s sculpture park, explore the historic Akershus Fortress or take a short ferry ride to the scenic islands for a taste of Nordic charm.

oxf.name: Oxford
oxf.text: Oxford, set in the heart of southern England on the River Thames, lies about 60 miles northwest of London. The city grew around the University of Oxford, founded in the 12th century and renowned as the oldest English-speaking university in the world. Today visitors can wander its historic cobbled streets, admire the dreaming spires of colleges such as Christ Church and Magdalen, and enjoy bustling market squares, independent bookshops and riverside punts. With a lively mix of academia, museums and cosy cafés, Oxford feels both timeless and vibrantly modern.

pap.name: Port-au-Prince
pap.text: Port-au-Prince sits on the Gulf of Caribbean on Haiti’s western coast, nestled between the sprawling hills of the Château de Mona and the bustling harbour that has long been the island’s gateway to the sea. Founded by French colonists in the 18th century, it became Haiti’s capital after independence in 1804 and later endured a devastating earthquake in 2010 that reshaped much of the city. Today the streets buzz with colourful market stalls, lively music and resilient locals; you can explore vibrant art galleries, sample hearty Haitian cuisine and feel the warm, welcoming spirit that pulses through the rebuilt neighbourhoods.

par.name: Paris
par.text: Paris, the capital of France, sits on the banks of the River Seine in the north-central part of the country. Founded by the Celtic Parisii tribe, it became an imperial centre when the Romans built Lutetia on the island now known as Île de la Cité, and it later grew into a hub of art, fashion and cuisine. Today the city dazzles visitors with its iconic skyline of Haussmannian boulevards, world-renowned museums such as the Louvre, and lively cafés spilling onto cobbled streets. A stroll along the Seine offers a mix of historic monuments, modern shops and the unmistakable buzz of a metropolis that still feels romantic and vibrant.

pat.name: Patras
pat.text: Patras sits on the north-west coast of the Peloponnese, perched on the Gulf of Patras and serving as a key gateway between Greece and Italy via its busy ferry terminal. It grew from an ancient Roman colony that became the chief port of the region of Achaea, and it is traditionally linked to Saint Andrew, who is said to have been martyred on a nearby hill in the first century. Today the city hums with a lively mix of historic stone façades, bustling markets and vibrant cafés, while the promenade along the waterfront offers striking sunset views and easy access to lively nightlife and cultural festivals.

pdl.name: Ponta Delgada
pdl.text: Ponta Delgada – the vibrant capital of Portugal’s Azores archipelago, perched on the southern coast of São Miguel Island.  Nestled in the mid‑Atlantic, this charming town blends volcanic landscapes with sweeping ocean views, a natural gateway between Europe and the Americas.  Founded in the 15th century by Portuguese settlers, it grew from a modest fishing village into a key stopover for trans‑Atlantic whalers and explorers, its historic cobblestone streets still echoing centuries of maritime heritage.  Today, Ponta Delgada thrives as a cultural hub—buzzing cafés, lively festivals, and eco‑tourism adventures—while preserving its rich past amid stunning cliffs, geothermal springs and world‑class cuisine.

pdx.name: Portland
pdx.text: Portland, Oregon, lies in the Pacific Northwest of the United States where the Willamette and Columbia rivers meet, about 70 miles east of the Pacific coast. Founded in 1845 and incorporated in 1851, the city grew around timber and river trade and later became known for its progressive urban planning. Today visitors find a vibrant mix of lush parks, bike-friendly streets and a thriving food scene, with famous coffee roasters, food-truck pods and a bustling Saturday market by the waterfront. The surrounding mountains and nearby vineyards add outdoor adventure and wine-tasting to the city’s laid-back, eco-conscious charm.

pee.name: Perm
pee.text: Perm lies on the banks of the wide, winding Kama River at the western foothills of the Ural Mountains, marking the traditional divide between European and Asian Russia. It was founded in 1723 as a modest settlement serving the salt-mining industry and grew into a key industrial hub during the 19th-century railway boom. Today the city offers a lively mix of cultural attractions – the striking Perm Opera and Ballet Theatre, the contemporary art-filled Perm Museum of Contemporary Art, and the open-air Koltushi Park – alongside cosy cafés and bustling markets, making a pleasant base for exploring both river scenery and the surrounding forested hills.

phc.name: Port Harcourt
phc.text: Port Harcourt, the bustling capital of Rivers State in southern Nigeria, sits on the banks of the Bonny River near the Niger Delta. Founded in 1912 by the British colonial administration, it was named after Lewis Vernon Harcourt, the then Secretary of State for the Colonies, and later grew into a major hub for Nigeria’s oil industry. Today the city blends modern high-rise office blocks with lively markets, waterfront promenades and a vibrant music scene; visitors can sample spicy river-fish dishes, explore the nearby mangrove forests and feel the energetic pulse of a town that is both a commercial powerhouse and a cultural gateway to the Delta.

phl.name: Philadelphia
phl.text: Philadelphia, nestled in the southeastern corner of Pennsylvania along the Delaware and Schuylkill rivers, is a city steeped in American history; it was the meeting place for the Continental Congress where the Declaration of Independence was debated and the Constitution signed. Today the streets buzz with a lively mix of historic cobblestones and modern skyscrapers, inviting visitors to stroll past the iconic Liberty Bell, explore world-class museums on the “Museum Mile,” and savour diverse food markets ranging from classic cheesesteaks to global street fare, all set against a backdrop of vibrant neighbourhoods and green riverfront parks.

phx.name: Phoenix
phx.text: Phoenix, Arizona, lies in the heart of the Sonoran Desert about 350 miles southeast of Las Vegas and 200 miles north of the Mexican border, cradled by the Salt River and surrounded by low mountains. Founded in 1867 as a farming community near the Hohokam canals, it grew into the capital of the territory and later the state in 1912. Today the city blends modern skyline and sprawling suburbs with desert-cactus scenery, offering vibrant arts districts, world-class museums and easy access to hiking in nearby Camelback Mountain, making it a warm, lively base for exploring the Southwest.

pit.name: Pittsburgh
pit.text: Pittsburgh, situated at the confluence of the Allegheny, Monongahela and Ohio rivers in western Pennsylvania, grew from a frontier fort into a powerhouse of industry in the 19th century, famously known for its steel production that earned the city the nickname “Steel City”. Today the skyline is a blend of historic brick warehouses and sleek glass towers, while the river valleys provide scenic bridges and bustling waterfront parks. Visitors can explore vibrant neighbourhoods such as the Strip District’s food markets, the cultural riches of the Carnegie museums, and enjoy a lively craft-beer scene against a backdrop of rolling hills.

ply.name: Plymouth
ply.text: Plymouth sits on the southern coast of Devon, where the River Plym meets the English Channel, and its natural harbour has been a gateway to the world for centuries. It is famously the departure point of the Mayflower in 1620, when the first group of Pilgrims set sail for North America. Today the city blends maritime heritage with a lively waterfront: you can wander along the historic Barbican, explore the National Marine Aquarium, and enjoy fresh seafood in bustling cafés while the modern shopping precincts and the iconic Smeaton’s Tower lighthouse remind you that Plymouth is both a historic port and a vibrant, contemporary destination.

pna.name: Patna
pna.text: Patna, the capital of Bihar in eastern India, sits on the south bank of the wide Ganges River and has been a centre of Indian life for millennia. Known in ancient times as Pataliputra, it was the capital of the Mauryan Empire under Emperor Ashoka, who built a famous stone pillar that still stands in the city. Today Patna blends its historic aura with lively street life: bustling bazaars sell everything from silk saris to spicy snacks, the Bihar Museum showcases artefacts spanning pre-historic to modern times, and the expansive Gandhi Maidan offers a green respite where locals gather for concerts, fairs and evening walks.

pnq.name: Pune
pnq.text: Pune, a bustling city in the western state of Maharashtra, lies on the Deccan Plateau about 150 km southeast of Mumbai. It grew from the 17th-century Maratha stronghold of Shivaji’s son, who established the city as a centre of administration and learning. Today Pune mixes old and new: leafy avenues are lined with historic forts, colonial-era buildings and lively markets, while modern cafés, tech parks and universities give it a youthful, cosmopolitan vibe. Visitors can explore the tranquil Osho Garden, sample street-food delicacies such as misal pav, and enjoy the pleasant climate that makes strolling through its streets pleasant year-round.

poa.name: Porto Alegre
poa.text: Porto Alegre lies on the eastern bank of the Guaíba estuary in southern Brazil, at the foothills of the Serra Gaúcha. Founded in 1769 as a Portuguese military outpost, it later became the capital of the state of Rio Grande do Sul and a key centre for the gaucho culture that blends European, Indigenous and African influences. Today the city feels lively and cosmopolitan, with tree-lined avenues, bustling cafés and a vibrant arts scene; the historic centre offers colonial architecture, while the waterfront parks provide relaxed views of the water and a chance to sample the region’s famous barbecues and wine.

por.name: Portsmouth
por.text: Portsmouth is a bustling coastal city on the southern coast of England, set on a natural harbour at the tip of the Langstone Peninsula in Hampshire. It has a rich naval heritage; the world-famous HMS Victory, Admiral Nelson’s flagship at the Battle of Trafalgar, still lies in the historic dockyard. Today the city blends maritime history with a lively waterfront: you can wander the historic streets, explore museums and the modern shopping precinct, enjoy fresh seafood by the sea, and catch ferries to the Isle of Wight, all under a backdrop of striking Victorian architecture and vibrant waterfront parks.

pos.name: Port of Spain
pos.text: Port of Spain sits on the western coast of Trinidad, tucked against the sheltered Gulf of Paria and framed by the lush Northern Range. The town was founded by the Spanish in 1592 and later fell under British control in 1797, becoming the island’s administrative centre. Today it buzzes with a lively mix of cultures: colourful market stalls sell fresh fruit and handmade crafts, the waterfront promenade offers panoramic sea views, and the streets come alive with music and dance during the world-famous Carnival. Visitors enjoy a blend of historic colonial architecture, modern cafés and a warm, welcoming atmosphere.

pra.name: Prague
pra.text: Prague, the capital of Czechia, sits on the Vltava River in the heart of Central Europe, roughly halfway between Berlin and Vienna. First recorded as a fortified settlement in the 9th century, it became the seat of Holy Roman Emperors in the 14th century, a period that left the city awash with Gothic and Baroque splendour. Today, wandering its cobbled streets feels like stepping into a living museum: the historic Old Town Square bustles with cafés, the Charles Bridge offers sunrise views over red-brick rooftops, and the vibrant mix of museums, street music and lively pubs makes every corner feel both timeless and lively.

pse.name: Port Said
pse.text: Port Said sits at the northern entrance of the Suez Canal on the Mediterranean coast of Egypt, a bustling gateway where the sea meets the canal’s busy waterway. Founded in 1859 to serve the canal’s construction, it quickly grew into an international port and was a key base for the Allied forces during the 1948 Arab-Israeli conflict. Today the city blends historic charm with modern energy: you can wander the wide promenade lined with cafés, explore the lively souk for spices and crafts, and watch massive container ships glide past, while the sea breezes carry a sense of maritime adventure.

rak.name: Marrakech
rak.text: Marrakech, situated in the western foothills of the Atlas Mountains in southern Morocco, has been a centre of trade and culture since it was founded in the 11th century by the Almoravid dynasty. The city's historic medina, a UNESCO World-heritage site, still contains the famous Koutoubia Mosque and the lively Jemaa el-Fna square, where storytellers, musicians and food stalls create a sensory feast each evening. Today visitors can wander narrow souks selling spices, textiles and ceramics, enjoy rooftop cafés overlooking the red-sandstone walls, and take short trips to nearby gardens and desert landscapes, making it a memorable stop on any North-African itinerary.

rec.name: Recife
rec.text: Recife, the capital of Pernambuco on Brazil’s north-eastern Atlantic coast, sits where the Capibaribe River meets the sea and is criss-crossed by a network of historic waterways. In the 17th century the city was seized by the Dutch, who held it from 1630 until the Portuguese reconquest in 1654, leaving a legacy of forts and Dutch-style architecture in the neighbourhood of Recife Antigo. Today visitors can stroll along colourful colonial streets, watch the sunrise over Boa Viagem beach, sample lively frevo music in the streets, and enjoy riverside cafés while watching colourful boats glide through the canals.

rnd.name: Rostov-on-Don
rnd.text: Rostov-on-Don sits on the western bank of the Don River in southern Russia, a gateway to the vast steppe and the Black Sea coast. Founded in the mid-18th century as a fortress to protect the empire’s southern frontier, it grew into a bustling trade hub and today it buzzes with a lively mix of history and modernity. Visitors can wander the wide embankment lined with cafés, explore the striking Rostov Kremlin and its golden domes, and soak up the vibrant atmosphere of markets selling everything from fresh fish to traditional crafts, all under a warm, sun-lit sky.

rom.name: Rome
rom.text: Rome, the bustling capital of Italy, sits in the central part of the country on the banks of the Tiber River. It was the heart of the ancient Roman Empire, famed for landmarks such as the Colosseum, an arena built in the first century AD where gladiators once fought. Today the city blends its rich past with modern life: cobbled streets lead past bustling cafés, vibrant markets and stunning baroque churches, while locals and visitors alike enjoy leisurely walks past ruins, gelato in sunny piazzas and the lively hum of trams threading through centuries-old neighbourhoods.

ros.name: Roscoff
ros.text: Roscoff is a charming fishing port on the north-west coast of Brittany, France, facing the English Channel and just a short ferry ride from Plymouth. Founded in the Middle Ages, the town became famous in the 19th century as the departure point for the first regular trans-Channel steamship service, linking France and Britain. Today Roscoff delights visitors with its colourful harbour, slate-roofed houses and a bustling market where fresh seafood and the celebrated “Roscoff pink” seaweed are sold. Stroll along the promenade, explore the historic granite church and sample the local cider for a quintessential Breton experience.

rot.name: Rotterdam
rot.text: Rotterdam sits on the banks of the Nieuwe Maas in the western Netherlands, just a short train ride from The Hague and a half-hour from the North Sea coast. The city rose from the ashes after World War II when its historic centre was heavily bombed, prompting a bold rebuild that gave Rotterdam its striking modern skyline. Today, visitors can wander along the bustling waterfront, admire daring architecture such as the cube houses and Erasmus Bridge, and enjoy a lively mix of multicultural cafés, bustling markets and world-class museums, all set against the backdrop of the busy port that is the heart of Europe's shipping trade.

rou.name: Rouen
rou.text: Rouen, perched on the River Seine in north-western France, is the historic capital of Normandy, roughly an hour and a half by train from Paris. It was here in 1419 that Joan of Arc was tried and later executed, a moment that still haunts the city’s medieval streets. Today the town blends cobbled alleys and half-timbered houses with bustling cafés, a vibrant arts scene and impressive Gothic architecture such as the towering Notre-Dame Cathedral that famously inspired Monet’s series of paintings. A stroll through its markets, museums and riverfront promenades feels both timeless and lively.

rsl.name: Rosslare
rsl.text: Rosslare, perched on the south-eastern tip of County Wexford, looks out over the Atlantic and the narrow St Gillian’s Strait that separates Ireland from Wales. The town grew around Rosslare Harbour, which was opened in 1906 to serve the new steam-packet service to Fishguard and still handles daily ferries to Pembroke Dock. Today the harbour area is a bustling gateway for travelers, while the adjoining sandy beach and flat promenade invite leisurely strolls, and a handful of cosy cafés and traditional pubs offer a relaxed taste of coastal life.

rtr.name: Rotorua
rtr.text: Rotorua, situated in the heart of New Zealand’s North Island within the Bay of Plenty region and set on the southern shore of Lake Rotorua, has been a centre of Māori life for centuries, home to the Te Arawa iwi. European visitors arrived in the 1860s and the town was declared a tourist resort in 1882, recognising its dramatic geysers and sulphur springs. Today the city blends geothermal landscapes, thriving Māori cultural performances, lake-front cafés and adventure activities, making it a lively destination for travellers seeking natural wonder and authentic New Zealand hospitality.

sal.name: Salisbury
sal.text: Salisbury is a historic market city set on the River Avon in the heart of Wiltshire, about 80 miles west of London and a short drive south from the stone circles of Stonehenge. Founded in Saxon times, it became famous in the 13th century for its magnificent cathedral, which boasts the tallest spire in England and houses the original Magna Carta. Today the city feels relaxed yet lively, with its medieval streets lined with independent shops, cozy cafés and a bustling market hall; the cathedral’s clock tower offers sweeping views of the surrounding countryside, making a visit both scenic and steeped in history.

san.name: Santander
san.text: Santander, perched on the northern coast of Spain in the autonomous community of Cantabria, is a lively seaside town overlooking the Bay of Biscay. Founded by the Romans as Portus Victoriae, it later became an important port for the Spanish crown, and its historic centre still shows the influence of 19th-century expansion under Queen María de las Mercedes. Today the city mixes elegant Art-Deco architecture with a bustling promenade, golden beaches and a vibrant culinary scene centred on fresh anchovies and local cheeses. Visitors can stroll along the Magdalena Peninsula, explore the maritime museum and enjoy the relaxed, salty air of this charming coastal gem.

sbh.name: Sabha
sbh.text: Sabha is a town in the far-south of Libya, sitting on the edge of the Sahara near the borders with Niger and Chad. It grew around a caravan stop on the historic trade routes that linked the Mediterranean coast with sub-Saharan Africa, and in the early twentieth century it became a centre for the trans-Saharan ivory and slave trade before those practices were outlawed. Today the town is a modest, sun-baked settlement where palm-shaded markets sell dates and textiles, the surrounding desert offers striking sand dunes for day-trips, and a small museum displays artefacts from its trading past.

scu.name: Santiago de Cuba
scu.text: Santiago de Cuba, perched on the southeastern coast of the island at the mouth of the Bay of Santiago, is Cuba’s second-largest city and a lively gateway to the island’s Afro-Cuban heritage. Founded in 1515, it later became the cradle of the Cuban Revolution, with the iconic Castillo del Morro watching over the harbour where Fidel Castro’s forces entered the city in 1959. Today the streets pulse with the rhythms of son and salsa, colourful colonial façades line bustling markets, and the surrounding hills offer spectacular views, making a visit feel like stepping into a vibrant, living history book.

sdg.name: San Diego
sdg.text: San Diego lies on the southern coast of California, bordering the Pacific Ocean and just a short drive from the Mexican border. Founded as a Spanish mission in 1769, the city grew around the historic Presidio and became a key naval base in the 20th century. Today it feels relaxed yet vibrant, with sun-kissed beaches, a bustling waterfront at the Embarcadero, and a mix of cultural attractions from the lively Gaslamp Quarter to the world-class museums of Balboa Park. Warm weather, friendly locals and endless outdoor activities make it a pleasant stop for any traveller.

sdq.name: Santo Domingo
sdq.text: Santo Domingo sits on the southern coast of the Dominican Republic, overlooking the Caribbean Sea where the Ozama River meets the harbour. Founded in 1496, it is the oldest continuously inhabited European settlement in the Americas and its historic Zona Colonial is a UNESCO World Heritage site full of cobbled streets, colourful façades and the first cathedral of the New World. Today the city blends the old with the new: lively plazas buzz with street musicians, modern cafés line the Paseo de los Trinitarios, and rooftop bars offer sweeping views of the sparkling sea and bustling port.

sev.name: Seville
sev.text: Seville, situated on the banks of the Guadalquivir in the heart of Andalusia, was known to the Romans as Hispalis and later became the dazzling capital of Moorish Al-Andalus, its grand Giralda originally a minaret. Today the city blends its grand cathedral, the world’s largest Gothic church, with a lively tapas bar scene, bustling orange-tree lined plazas and nightly flamenco performances, while the annual Feria de Abril fills the streets with colour and music, making it a vibrant crossroads of history and modern Spanish life and warm hospitality for all.

sju.name: San Juan
sju.text: San Juan, the capital of Puerto Rico, sits on the island’s north-eastern coast overlooking the Atlantic. Founded by Spanish colonists in 1521, the city grew around the fortified walls of Old San Juan, where the 16th-century Castillo San Felipe del Morro and the massive San Cristóbal fort still dominate the skyline. Today it blends historic cobblestones with a waterfront, trendy cafés and an arts scene, while its beaches and colourful street life attract visitors from around the world. The mix of colonial charm and energy makes it an unforgettable destination.

slc.name: Salt Lake City
slc.text: Salt Lake City lies in the north-western corner of the United States, nestled at the foot of the Wasatch Mountains and alongside the great Great Salt Lake in Utah. Founded in 1847 by Mormon pioneers led by Brigham Young, it quickly grew into a hub for westward settlers and the trans-continental railroad. Today the city blends modern skyscrapers with historic temples, offering easy access to outdoor adventures such as skiing, hiking and lake-side cycling, while its lively downtown boasts museums, a vibrant food scene and a welcoming, laid-back atmosphere.

sli.name: Saint-Louis
sli.text: Saint-Louis lies on the north-west coast of Senegal, perched on the left bank of the River Senegal just a short ferry ride from the capital Dakar. Founded in the 17th century as a French trading post, it became the capital of French West Africa in the 19th century before the seat moved to Dakar. Today the town is a charming blend of colonial architecture and lively markets: pastel-coloured houses line narrow streets, the historic Island of Saint-Louis offers cobbled lanes, museums and cafés, and the Atlantic breezes make evening walks along the waterfront especially pleasant.

smf.name: Sacramento
smf.text: Sacramento, the capital city of California, sits where the Sacramento and American Rivers meet in the heart of the state's fertile Central Valley. It grew rapidly during the Gold Rush, becoming the state capital in 1854 and preserving much of its 19th-century charm in the cobbled streets of Old Sacramento. Today the city offers a pleasant mix of history and modernity: riverfront parks invite picnics and kayaking, a lively farm-to-table restaurant scene showcases local produce, and museums such as the California State Railroad Museum and the Crocker Art Museum provide engaging cultural stops, all set against a backdrop of sunny skies and friendly locals.

sof.name: Sofia
sof.text: Sofia, the capital of Bulgaria, lies in the western part of the country at the foot of Vitosha Mountain, where the Iskar River winds through a broad valley. It has been inhabited since antiquity, and the city’s name first appears in Roman records as Serdica, a key centre of the empire in the fourth century. Today Sofia blends leafy boulevards, lively cafés and impressive Orthodox churches with the modern buzz of museums, galleries and a growing tech scene; a short funicular ride takes you up Vitosha for panoramic views and fresh mountain air, making a visit feel both historic and contemporary.

sou.name: Southampton
sou.text: Southampton, a port city on England’s south-coast, lies on the northern shore of the Solent where the River Itchen meets the sea. It is famous as the departure point for the RMS Titanic in 1912, a historic moment that still echoes in the city's maritime museums. Today the waterfront buzzes with a mix of modern waterfront bars, historic dockside warehouses and the vibrant cultural quarter around the old medieval walls. Visitors can wander the bustling market, explore the SeaCity Museum, enjoy a stroll along the historic Ocean Village marina, and take a short ferry ride to the Isle of Wight, all set against a backdrop of lively cafés and a friendly, bustling atmosphere.

spl.name: Split
spl.text: Split sits on the sparkling Adriatic coast of Croatia, roughly halfway between the Istrian peninsula and the island of Hvar, and it is the country’s second-largest city. Its heart is the massive Diocletian’s Palace, a 4th-century Roman imperial complex that still forms the bustling old town, a UNESCO World Heritage site that still houses shops, homes and cafés within its ancient walls. Today visitors wander the marble streets, enjoy fresh seafood on the Riva promenade, and can easily hop on ferries to nearby islands, while the Mediterranean climate, lively markets and striking sea views give the city a vibrant, relaxed atmosphere.

srg.name: Sorong
srg.text: Sorong – perched on the western tip of New Guinea, this bustling port city greets you where the warm waters of the Raja Ampat archipelago meet the vast expanse of the Pacific. Once a modest Dutch outpost in the early 1900s, Sorong grew into a strategic gateway during World War II and later became the commercial heart of West Papua. Today it pulses with modern energy: a hub for oil and gas, a launchpad for divers diving into world‑renowned coral reefs, and a cultural crossroads where indigenous traditions mingle with vibrant street markets. Join us as we explore the charm and promise of Sorong, Indonesia’s hidden coastal gem.

sth.name: Stockholm
sth.text: Stockholm, the capital of Sweden, spreads across 14 islands where the Baltic Sea meets Lake Mälaren in the eastern part of the country. First mentioned in a 13th-century charter, the city grew around the medieval Gamla Stan, its cobbled old town centred on the 13th-century St Nicholas Church and the Royal Palace. Today Stockholm feels clean and relaxed yet vibrant, with sleek waterfront promenades, leafy parks and a thriving café culture; you can wander from historic alleys to cutting-edge museums such as the Fotografiska, hop on a ferry to explore the archipelago, and enjoy long summer evenings illuminated by countless lanterns.

stj.name: Santiago
stj.text: Santiago de los Caballeros, nestled in the fertile Cibao valley of the Dominican Republic’s north-central plateau, is the island’s second-largest city and a hub of coffee and cacao production. Founded in the late-15th century, it later became the centre of the 19th-century Restoration War, a fact commemorated by the towering Monument to the Heroes of the Restoration that dominates the skyline. Today the city blends colonial charm with modern vibrancy: colourful market stalls line the bustling streets, lively cafés serve strong coffee, and the surrounding mountains offer scenic drives and opportunities to taste the region’s renowned rum and fresh tropical fruit.

stl.name: St Louis
stl.text: St Louis lies on the western bank of the Mississippi River in the heart of the American Midwest, about 300 miles west of the Illinois border. Founded in 1764 by French fur traders, the city grew around the historic Gateway Arch, a 630-foot stainless-steel monument that commemorates the westward expansion of the United States. Today visitors can stroll along the vibrant Riverfront, explore world-class museums such as the St Louis Art Museum and the Science Centre, and savour famous barbecue in the bustling downtown districts, all while enjoying the city’s blend of historic brick warehouses and modern skyline.

str.name: Strasbourg
str.text: Strasbourg, perched on the banks of the River Ill where France meets Germany, is the capital of the Alsace region in north-eastern France. Founded as a Roman settlement, it later became an Imperial Free City of the Holy Roman Empire and was a key centre of the Reformation, hosting the famous 1529 Diet of Augsburg delegates. Today the city charms visitors with its UNESCO-listed Grande Île, where the timber-framed “half-timber” houses line cobbled streets and the stunning Gothic cathedral towers above the bustling markets. A blend of French and German cuisine, lively cafés and modern European institutions makes Strasbourg a vibrant, walkable destination.

tao.name: Qingdao
tao.text: Qingdao, a coastal city in Shandong province on China’s Yellow Sea, is famed for its blend of German colonial heritage and modern seaside charm. Founded as a fishing village, it became a German concession in 1898, which left the striking red-tiled roofs of the former Governor’s Hall and the historic Badaguan neighbourhood. Today visitors can stroll along the bustling waterfront promenade, sip locally brewed Tsingtao beer in lively pubs, wander the fragrant jasmine-lined streets, and enjoy fresh seafood while taking in the backdrop of gentle hills and crystal-clear bays.

tfs.name: Santa Cruz de Tenerife
tfs.text: Santa Cruz de Tenerife – perched on the northeast coast of Spain’s sun‑kissed Canary Islands, this vibrant city greets you with volcanic horizons and Atlantic breezes. Founded in the 16th century as a modest port for sugar and wine, it soon blossomed into a bustling gateway for explorers heading to the New World. Today, Santa Cruz is the archipelago’s political and cultural heart, famed for its colorful Carnaval, bustling Mercado de Nuestra Señora de África, and striking modern architecture like the Auditorio de Tenerife. From historic plazas to lively waterfront cafés, the city perfectly blends heritage with contemporary island charm.

ths.name: Thessaloniki
ths.text: Thessaloniki, Greece’s vibrant second-city, sits on the north-eastern edge of the Thermaic Gulf at the foot of Mount Horti, where the Aegean Sea meets the inland plains of Central Macedonia. Founded in 315 BC by Cassander, it soon became a crucial Roman and Byzantine port and later the capital of the short-lived Kingdom of Thessalonica. Today the city buzzes with a lively waterfront promenade, bustling markets and a mix of Ottoman, Byzantine and modernist architecture; cafés spill onto the streets, the scent of fresh seafood drifts from tavernas, and the annual film festival adds a cosmopolitan sparkle to its historic charm.

tip.name: Tripoli
tip.text: Tripoli, the capital of Libya, lies on the central Mediterranean coast where the ancient Phoenician harbour merges with the modern cityscape. Founded in the 7th century BC, it later became the bustling centre of the Ottoman province of Tripolitania and still retains parts of the historic Medina with its narrow alleys and Ottoman-era forts. Today visitors find a blend of sandy beaches, vibrant souks selling spices and textiles, and a waterfront promenade lined with cafés offering fresh seafood. The city’s lively markets, colonial-style cafés and nearby ruins give a vivid glimpse of its layered past while providing a welcoming, cosmopolitan atmosphere.

tkd.name: Takoradi
tkd.text: Takoradi, a bustling coastal town in the Western Region of Ghana, lies on the Atlantic shoreline about 220 km west of Accra and forms part of the twin city Sekondi-Takoradi. Founded in the 19th century as a harbour for the export of cocoa and timber, it later became a key naval base during World War II, a role that still echoes in its historic fort and museum. Today the town buzzes with colourful markets, lively street food stalls serving grilled fish and jollof rice, and a laid-back waterfront where palm-shaded promenades invite visitors to watch ferries and fishing boats glide by, offering a warm mix of commerce, culture and seaside charm.

tls.name: Toulouse
tls.text: Toulouse, in southwestern France, lies on the banks of the Garonne River about 150 km east of the Atlantic coast. Known as “La Ville Rose” for its distinctive pink-hued bricks, the city was a centre of medieval commerce and later became a hub of the aerospace industry, home to the headquarters of Airbus. Visitors today can wander its historic centre, admire the towering Saint-Sernin basilica, and relax in lively cafés lining the riverfront, while the modern university atmosphere adds a youthful buzz to the charming, sun-lit streets.

tng.name: Tangier
tng.text: Tangier, perched on the north-western tip of Morocco where the Mediterranean meets the Atlantic, has long been a gateway between Europe and Africa. Historically it was a key port for Phoenician traders and later became famous in the 20th century as an international zone that attracted artists, writers and spies. Today the town bustles with colourful souks, sleek cafés overlooking the Strait and a mix of modern hotels beside restored medina streets; you can wander the Kasbah for sweeping sea views, sample fresh seafood in the harbour, and feel the relaxed, multicultural rhythm that still defines this historic crossroads.

tof.name: Tomsk
tof.text: Tomsk lies in western Siberia, on the banks of the Tom River about 650 km east of the Ural Mountains and roughly 2 000 km northeast of Moscow. Founded in 1604 as a fort on the Siberian trade route, it is one of the oldest towns in the region and today hosts Russia’s first university, established in 1888. Visitors find a lively mix of historic wooden houses, leafy avenues and modern cafés, while the riverfront offers pleasant walks and occasional boat trips. Museums, theatres and a vibrant student community give the city a youthful, cultural buzz that contrasts pleasantly with its frontier heritage.

tou.name: Tours
tou.text: Tours, set on the gentle bend of the River Loire in the heart of France’s historic Centre-Val de Loire, is a lively gateway to the country’s famed châteaux. Its medieval old town grew around the impressive Saint-Gatien cathedral, which dates back to the 12th century and bears the marks of the Hundred Years’ War. Today the city blends that rich heritage with a bustling, contemporary vibe: cobbled streets are lined with cafés and boutique shops, the vibrant market on Place Plumereau hums with locals, and river cruises offer relaxed views of the surrounding vineyards. Tours feels both comfortably historic and refreshingly modern, making it a pleasant stop for any traveller.

tpa.name: Tampa
tpa.text: Tampa sits on the western edge of Florida, straddling the Hillsborough River where it meets the Gulf of Mexico, and is the largest city in the Tampa Bay area. The settlement began as Fort Brooke in 1824, later growing into a bustling port and, in the late-19th century, becoming famous for its thriving cigar factories in Ybor City, a neighbourhood founded by Cuban and Spanish immigrants. Today the city offers a lively mix of modern skyline, waterfront parks and a lively historic quarter, while nearby sandy beaches, Busch Gardens and a diverse food scene make a visit both relaxed and exciting.

tsn.name: Tianjin
tsn.text: Tianjin, a bustling port city in northern China, sits on the banks of the Hai River about 120 kilometres southeast of Beijing. It grew into a major treaty port after the Opium Wars, when foreign concessions were established in the 19th century, leaving a distinctive mix of European-style architecture and traditional Chinese streets. Today the city blends sleek skyscrapers with historic districts such as the Italian-style St Leonardo’s Avenue, offering lively food markets, river cruises, and modern art galleries. Visitors can savour fresh seafood, wander the colourful hutongs and enjoy a vibrant nightlife that reflects both its rich past and its fast-moving present.

tun.name: Tunis
tun.text: Tunis, the bustling capital of Tunisia, sits on the north-eastern edge of the country where the Mediterranean Sea meets the fertile plain of the Gulf of Tunis. Founded by the Phoenicians and later becoming a major centre of the Roman province of Africa, its medina still contains the impressive 9th-century Great Mosque of Al-Zaytuna. Today the city blends ancient winding alleys with modern cafés, lively souks and a vibrant waterfront promenade; you can wander past Ottoman-era palaces, sample fragrant harissa-spiced dishes, and enjoy sweeping sea views from the nearby Carthage ruins.

tur.name: Turin
tur.text: Turin, nestled in the north-west of Italy at the foot of the Alps and straddling the Po River, was the first capital of a unified Italy in 1861 and retains grand boulevards reminiscent of its regal past. Today the city blends elegant baroque architecture with a lively café culture; you can sip an espresso beside the Mole Antonelliana, explore the sleek museums of contemporary art, and wander the leafy Valentino Park. Its bustling markets, Michelin-starred chocolate shops and vibrant university atmosphere make Turin a warm, cosmopolitan stop for any traveller.

tus.name: Tucson
tus.text: Tucson, nestled in the southern part of Arizona about 60 miles north of the Mexican border, lies at the edge of the Sonoran Desert and is framed by the Santa Catalina, Rincon and Tucson Mountains. The town began as a Spanish presidio in 1775, making it one of the oldest European-settled communities in the American Southwest. Today the city blends desert scenery with a lively cultural scene: you can wander historic Fourth Avenue, explore the University of Arizona’s museums, admire towering saguaro cacti in Saguaro National Park, and enjoy a thriving food and arts scene that feels both relaxed and surprisingly cosmopolitan.

tzx.name: Trabzon
tzx.text: Trabzon sits on the Black Sea coast of north-eastern Turkey, framed by lush hills and the Pontic Mountains. Founded as the Greek colony Trapezus in the 8th century BC, it later became an important stop on the Silk Road and the site of the famous Sumela Monastery, perched on a cliff overlooking the surrounding forest. Today the city offers a pleasant mix of sea-front promenades, lively fish markets and Ottoman-era tea houses where you can sample the local Black Sea tea. The backdrop of mist-y mountains and the scent of fresh seafood make a visit both relaxing and memorable.

ufa.name: Ufa
ufa.text: Ufa, the capital of Bashkortostan in the western foothills of the Ural Mountains, sits on the banks of the Belaya River about 1,200 km east of Moscow. Founded in 1574 as a Russian fortress, it later became an important centre for oil production in the early 20th century, shaping its industrial heritage. Today the city blends Soviet-era architecture with vibrant cultural life: you can stroll along the river promenade, explore the colourful Bashkir State Museum, and sample hearty Tatar and Bashkir cuisine in bustling cafés, while the surrounding hills offer easy hikes and a refreshing contrast to the urban bustle.

uio.name: Quito
uio.text: Quito, the capital of Ecuador, sits high in the Andes at an altitude of about 2,850 metres, making it one of the world’s highest capital cities. Founded by the Spanish in 1534, it preserves a remarkably intact colonial centre that was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1978, with churches, plazas and narrow cobbled streets that echo the city’s 16th-century past. Today visitors find a vibrant mix of old and new: bustling markets selling fresh fruit and handmade crafts, modern cafés perched on sun-lit terraces, and a backdrop of snow-capped volcanoes that frame the city’s lively streets and friendly atmosphere.

val.name: Valencia
val.text: Valencia, Spain, sits on the eastern Mediterranean coast where the Turia River meets the sea, about three hours by train south of Barcelona. Founded as a Roman colony in the second century BC, the city later flourished under Moorish rule and retained its medieval walls, parts of which you can still see strolling through the historic centre. Today Valencia feels vibrant and laid-back: you can wander the futuristic City of Arts and Sciences, sip a chilled horchata in a sun-dappled plaza, or wander the bustling Central Market, all while the scent of paella drifting from seaside restaurants reminds you why this port city is a favourite stop for travellers.

ven.name: Venice
ven.text: Venice, a city of islands in the north-east of Italy, sits in the shallow lagoon of the Adriatic Sea and is linked by more than 400 bridges and narrow canals. It was a powerful maritime republic from the Middle Ages, dominating trade between Europe and the East and famed for its elaborate glassmaking on the island of Murano. Today, visitors wander past bustling markets and quiet back-streets, glide beneath elegant arched bridges in a vapour-rising gondola, and enjoy coffee in historic squares where the scent of fresh seafood mixes with the echo of centuries-old bells.

vie.name: Vienna
vie.text: Vienna, the capital of Austria, lies in the country’s eastern corner along the Danube River, framed by the Alpine foothills. It was the imperial seat of the Habsburg dynasty for centuries, and its historic centre still bears the grandeur of that era with baroque palaces such as the Hofburg and the stunning State Opera House. Today the city blends this regal past with a lively, modern vibe: coffee houses hum with conversation, museums showcase works from Klimt to contemporary artists, and the streets are lined with markets, parks and efficient tram lines that make exploring a pleasure for any visitor.

war.name: Warsaw
war.text: Warsaw, the capital of Poland, sits on the banks of the Vistula River in the east-central part of the country. The city’s Old Town, with its colourful townhouses and cobbled squares, was painstakingly rebuilt after being razed during the Second World War and is now a UNESCO World Heritage site. Today Warsaw buzzes with a lively mix of history and modernity: sleek skyscrapers rise beside grand palaces, world-class museums sit alongside bustling cafés, and the numerous parks and river promenades make it a pleasant place to wander and soak up both Polish culture and contemporary European flair.

wdh.name: Windhoek
wdh.text: Windhoek, the capital of Namibia, sits in the central highlands at an altitude of about 1 700 metres, framed by the rugged Dâures and Khomas mountains. Founded in 1840 as a small settlement of the Herero people, it later became a German colonial outpost, and many red-brick buildings from that era still line its streets. Today the city blends colonial charm with modern African energy: lively cafés serve local coffee, the bustling craft market offers woven blankets and jewellery, and the surrounding semi-desert scenery makes a striking backdrop for relaxed strolls through tree-lined avenues and historic plazas.

xmn.name: Xiamen
xmn.text: Xiamen, a bustling coastal city in Fujian province on China’s southeast seaboard, sits opposite the Taiwan Strait and is linked to the historic Gulangyu Island by a short ferry ride. It became a treaty port in the mid-19th century after the First Opium War, which sparked its development as a centre of overseas trade. Today the city charms visitors with palm-shaded promenades, a lively pedestrian street full of street food stalls, well-preserved temples and modern cafés, and a pleasant subtropical climate that makes exploring its harbourside parks and colourful neighbourhoods a relaxed delight.

yae.name: Yaounde
yae.text: Yaoundé, the capital of Cameroon, sits on a series of hills in the central part of the country, about 750 km east of the Atlantic coast. Founded in 1888 as a German outpost, it became the administrative centre of French Cameroon after World War I and was declared the national capital in 1960. Today the city buzzes with a mix of modern cafés, bustling markets and leafy avenues shaded by jacaranda trees; you can wander the lively neighbourhood of Mfoundi, sample local dishes such as ndolé, and enjoy panoramic views of the surrounding plateau from the hilltop park near the presidential palace.

yfc.name: Fredericton
yfc.text: Fredericton, the capital city of New Brunswick, lies on the banks of the Saint John River in the heart of the province’s western valley. Founded in 1785 and named after Prince Frederick, the town grew around a Loyalist settlement and later became a centre for the province’s timber trade, a heritage still hinted at in its historic wooden warehouses.
