Today visitors can stroll along the riverfront promenade, explore the striking Legislative Assembly building and vibrant downtown filled with galleries, cafés and the University of New Brunswick campus, all set against a backdrop of leafy parks and gentle river views.

yks.name: Yakutsk
yks.text: Yakutsk, perched on the banks of the Lena River in the heart of Siberia, is the capital of the Sakha Republic and one of the world’s coldest cities, where winter temperatures regularly plunge below –40 °C. Founded in 1632 as a Russian outpost, it grew into a centre for the fur trade and later for diamond mining, which still fuels the local economy. Today the town is a surprising blend of modernity and tradition: colourful wooden houses line lively streets, museums showcase indigenous Yakut culture, and a hearty cuisine of reindeer and fish warms visitors after a crisp, clear-air stroll beneath snow-capped hills.

yok.name: Yokohama
yok.text: Yokohama, the bustling port city just a half‑hour train ride south of Tokyo, greets travelers with a perfect blend of sea‑sprayed charm and modern flair. Founded as a modest fishing village, it exploded onto the world stage in 1859 when the Treaty of Kanagawa opened its harbor to foreign trade, sparking the iconic Red Brick Warehouses and the lively foreign‑settlement vibe that still lingers today. Today, Yokohama is Japan’s second‑largest city, a hub of technology, fashion and gastronomy—home to the towering Landmark Tower, the serene Sankeien Garden, and a famed Chinatown that serves up some of the country’s best dumplings. Join us as we explore this dynamic gateway between tradition and tomorrow.

yor.name: York
yor.text: York, a historic city in North Yorkshire, lies at the confluence of the Rivers Ouse and Foss, about 30 miles north-east of Leeds and 190 miles north of London. Founded by the Romans as Eboracum, it later became a key Viking-era centre and the site of the famous medieval York Minster. Today the walled city feels compact and lively: you can wander the cobbled Shambles, explore the National Railway Museum, and enjoy the vibrant cafés and independent shops that spill onto the ancient streets, while the impressive city walls offer pleasant walks with views over the modern town below.

yqr.name: Regina
yqr.text: Regina, the capital of Saskatchewan in Canada, sits on the flat, golden prairie plain about 190 kilometres south of the province’s northern border and 250 kilometres north of the United States. The city grew from a railway settlement founded in 1882 and was promptly chosen as the provincial capital, a status it retains today. Its most striking landmark is the grand sandstone Legislative Building, whose copper dome can be seen from many points in town. Modern visitors find a friendly, laid-back atmosphere, with excellent museums, a vibrant culinary scene and wide-open riverfront parks that showcase the sweeping skies and endless horizons of the Canadian West.

yqt.name: Thunder Bay
yqt.text: Thunder Bay sits on the north-western shore of Lake Superior in Ontario, Canada, where the Kaministiquia River meets the lake’s vast waters. The city grew from the historic fur-trading outpost of Fort William, a key Hudson’s Bay Company centre in the early 1800s that helped open the interior to European trade. Today the town blends rugged natural beauty with a relaxed, welcoming vibe: you can stroll along the waterfront boardwalk, explore the striking rock formations of the nearby Sleeping Giant, enjoy Indigenous art galleries and sample fresh lake fish in cosy cafés, all under a backdrop of striking shoreline and pine-clad hills.

yxe.name: Saskatoon
yxe.text: Saskatoon sits on the east bank of the South Saskatchewan River in the central part of the Canadian province of Saskatchewan, roughly midway between Calgary and Winnipeg. Founded in the late 19th century, the town grew around a North West Company trading post and was officially incorporated in 1906, becoming a key hub for grain and railway traffic on the Canadian Prairies. Today visitors find a vibrant mix of modern cafés, art galleries and riverside parks, with the striking skyline reflected in the river’s waters and a lively cultural scene that celebrates both its Indigenous heritage and its pioneering past.

yxy.name: Whitehorse
yxy.text: Whitehorse, the capital of Yukon in north-west Canada, sits on the banks of the mighty Yukon River about 30 kilometres south of the Alaska border. It grew from a modest river-crossing called “the White Horse Rapids” into a bustling supply hub during the Klondike Gold Rush of the late 1890s, when prospectors streamed through on their way to the goldfields. Today the town blends frontier charm with modern comforts: colourful storefronts line Main Street, the Yukon Beringia Interpretive Centre showcases ancient fossils, and the surrounding mountains and river offer spectacular hiking, wildlife spotting and, in winter, brilliant aurora borealis displays.

yyg.name: Charlottetown
yyg.text: Charlottetown, the capital of Prince Edward Island, sits on the southern shore of the island at the head of Charlottetown Harbour, where the Northumberland Strait meets the Gulf of St Lawrence. In 1864 the town hosted the Charlottetown Conference, the first meeting that set the foundations for Canadian Confederation, earning it the nickname “Birthplace of Confederation”. Today the city blends historic charm with a lively modern vibe: colourful Victorian houses line the waterfront, boutique shops and cafés spill onto pedestrian streets, and the bustling summer festivals fill the air with music and the scent of fresh seafood, making a visit both relaxed and culturally rich.

yzd.name: Yazd
yzd.text: Yazd, a desert city in central Iran about 250 km south-east of Tehran, sits on the edge of the Dasht-e Kavir plain. It is famous for its ancient mud-brick architecture and was a centre of Zoroastrian worship long before the Islamic era, with the historic Fahadan quarter preserving narrow alleys and wind-catchers that date back to the 12th century. Today the town feels calm and sun-warmed; you can wander its quiet bazaars, sip tea in a courtyard shaded by towering qanats, and watch the sunset turn the ochre roofs into a golden glow, while modern cafés and museums sit alongside the timeless adobe walls.

yzf.name: Yellowknife
yzf.text: Yellowknife, the capital of Canada’s Northwest Territories, sits on the northern shore of Great Slave Lake, just below the Arctic Circle. Founded in the 1930s during the region’s gold-rush, the town was named after the Yellowknife Dene, whose traditional lands include the area. Today the city is a vibrant mix of modern amenities and wilderness adventure, offering museums that showcase Indigenous culture and mining history, colourful waterfront promenades, and easy access to spectacular northern lights, dog-sledding and canoe trips on the lake, all set against a backdrop of boreal forest and crisp, clean air.

zag.name: Zagreb
zag.text: Zagreb, the capital of Croatia, sits in the north-west of the country where the Sava and Medveščak rivers meet, a short drive from the Slovenian border and the Adriatic coast. First mentioned in a 1093 charter, the city grew around the medieval Kaptol cathedral district and later became a key Habsburg administrative centre. Today Zagreb buzzes with a relaxed yet lively atmosphere: its pedestrian-only Ban Jelačić Square hosts cafés, street musicians and markets, while the Upper Town offers cobbled lanes, museums and stunning views of the red-tiled roofs that stretch beneath the surrounding hills.

zar.name: Zaragoza
zar.text: Zaragoza, nestled in the north-east of Spain on the banks of the Ebro River, lies roughly halfway between Madrid and Barcelona and serves as the capital of the autonomous community of Aragon. The city’s most famous landmark, the Basilica of Our Lady of the Pillar, has been a major pilgrimage site since the early medieval period, when legend says the Virgin Mary appeared to the apostle James here. Today Zaragoza buzzes with a lively mix of historic charm and modern energy: you can stroll through bustling tapas bars, explore the Roman-era Aljafería Palace, and enjoy riverside walks while the city’s vibrant cultural calendar offers festivals, music and art throughout the year.

zrh.name: Zurich
zrh.text: Zurich lies in the north-east of Switzerland, nestled at the tip of Lake Zürich and framed by the Limmat River and the Swiss Alps. First mentioned in a document of 846 AD, the city grew around a Benedictine abbey that became a centre of trade and later a hub of the Reformation. Today Zurich blends historic charm with modern vitality: you can wander the well-preserved medieval Altstadt, admire art at the Kunsthaus, and savour coffee in stylish cafés while the efficient trams whisk you past gleaming banks, bustling markets and tranquil lakeside promenades.
